BUYING GUIDES

A shortlist should explain the trade-offs.

Turn a long manufacturer directory into a small set of candidates worth evaluating.

THE KEY IDEA

Separate mandatory requirements, useful preferences, and unresolved questions before scoring candidates.

A large manufacturer directory is useful for discovery. It becomes a buying tool only when a team can explain why particular platforms remain on the shortlist. That explanation should survive beyond the person who first collected the links, especially when technical and procurement teams evaluate different parts of the decision.

01

Use requirements before rankings

Write down the conditions a platform must satisfy to enter the evaluation. Keep preferences in a separate list. Otherwise, an appealing feature can compensate for a missing requirement in a scoring sheet even though it cannot compensate for it in the real application.

02

Track the exact model

A company may offer multiple hardware families or generations. Record the representative model, configuration, and official source for each candidate. Do not mix specifications from one generation with prices or availability statements for another. Manufacturer names alone are not precise enough for a technical comparison.

03

Treat missing information consistently

Use a visible “not confirmed” state. Assign an owner to important unanswered questions and establish whether they must be resolved before a trial or before purchase. Avoid guessing values simply to make every row look complete. A clear gap can guide the next supplier conversation.

04

Keep the comparison small and revisable

Select a few candidates that represent meaningful trade-offs, such as development access, support, or suitability for the workspace. Revisit the shortlist when evidence changes. The aim is a better decision process, not a permanent leaderboard of companies with different products and commercial stages.

MAKE IT PRACTICAL

Your next step.

  • Separate requirements from preferences.
  • Link every record to an exact model.
  • Give important unknowns an owner and a deadline.
